Which state capital sits on the estuary of the Derwent River?
fact: Founded in 1804, Hobart is Australia's second-oldest capital city.

text: Leaving out Antarctica, Australia's highest peak, Mawson Peak, is on which island?
fact: Mawson Peak is an active volcano, about 500 m higher than Mount Kosciuszko.

text: Kata Tjuta in the Northern Territory was long known by what English name?
fact: Kata Tjuta means "many heads" in the local Pitjantjatjara language.

text: Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre, Australia's largest lake, lies in which state?
fact: Its floor dips to about 15 m below sea level, the lowest point in Australia.

text: Rottnest Island, famous for its quokkas, lies off the coast near which city?
fact: Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh mistook quokkas for rats and called it "Rats' Nest Island".

text: The Great Ocean Road is a memorial to those who died in which conflict?
fact: About 3000 returned soldiers built it between 1919 and 1932.

text: After Western Australia, which is Australia's largest state or territory by area?
fact: Queensland covers about 1.7 million square kilometres.

text: The striped beehive domes of the Bungle Bungle Range are in which national park?
fact: Though Aboriginal people knew them for millennia, the domes were little known until the 1980s.

text: The Big Merino, a 15-metre concrete sheep, stands in which NSW city?
fact: Locals call him "Rambo". He opened in 1985 and was moved to a new site in 2007.

text: Broken Hill is in NSW but follows the time zone and daylight saving of which state?
fact: The town's closest links were with Adelaide, so it kept Central time.

text: Who commanded the First Fleet and became the first Governor of New South Wales?
fact: Phillip chose Sydney Cove after finding Botany Bay unsuitable.

text: Ned Kelly's gang made their last stand in 1880 at which Victorian town?
fact: Kelly wore homemade armour made from plough mouldboards.

text: The Burke and Wills expedition set out in 1860 from which city?
fact: Their aim was to cross the continent to the Gulf of Carpentaria.

text: Which Governor-General dismissed Prime Minister Gough Whitlam in 1975?
fact: Whitlam famously said, "Well may we say God save the Queen".

text: Which colony's 1894 law gave women both the vote and the right to stand for parliament?
Which navigator first sailed around Australia and popularised its name?
fact: Flinders circumnavigated the continent in 1802–03 aboard HMS Investigator.

text: Who left an inscribed pewter plate on an island in Shark Bay in 1616?
fact: It is the oldest known surviving artefact of European exploration in Australia.

text: In February 1942, which Australian city was bombed by Japanese aircraft?
fact: More bombs were dropped on Darwin on 19 February than on Pearl Harbor.

text: The landmark 1992 Mabo case concerned land on which Torres Strait island?
fact: The High Court rejected the idea that Australia was terra nullius, "land belonging to no one".

text: Who led the 1966 Wave Hill walk-off by Gurindji stockmen?
fact: In 1975 Gough Whitlam poured soil into Lingiari's hand to mark the return of land.

text: The 1932 "Emu War", in which soldiers with machine guns fought emus, was in which state?
fact: Despite thousands of rounds fired, the emus are widely seen as the winners.

text: The equestrian events of the 1956 Melbourne Olympics were held in which city?
fact: Australia's strict quarantine rules meant foreign horses couldn't come.

text: Which woman, the first elected to an Australian parliament, appears on the $50 note?
fact: Cowan won a seat in Western Australia's parliament in 1921.

text: Opera star Nellie Melba took her stage name from which city?
fact: She was born Helen Porter Mitchell in Richmond, Victoria, in 1861.

text: Who was the first Aboriginal Australian to sit in federal parliament?
fact: Bonner joined the Senate for Queensland in 1971.

text: What was the name of the plane that made the first flight from the US to Australia in 1928?
fact: Charles Kingsford Smith and his crew flew from California to Brisbane in three hops.

text: Racehorse Phar Lap was foaled in which country?
fact: He died suddenly in California, soon after winning a race in Mexico.

text: Which poet wrote "My Country", with the line "I love a sunburnt country"?
fact: Mackellar wrote it in England, aged 19. It was first published in 1908.

text: Which Australian novelist won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1973?
fact: White used his prize money to set up an award for overlooked Australian writers.

text: Adelaide-born Howard Florey shared a Nobel Prize for turning what into a usable drug?
fact: He shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

text: Australian scientist David Warren invented which aviation device?
fact: His idea came after investigating a 1953 Comet airliner crash.

text: Who designed the Aboriginal flag in 1971?
fact: Bernard Namok designed the Torres Strait Islander flag in 1992.

text: Sydney Opera House architect Jørn Utzon came from which country?
fact: Utzon left the project in 1966 and never saw the finished building in person.

text: Cathy Freeman won gold at the Sydney 2000 Olympics in which event?
fact: She won the final in 49.11 seconds.

text: Which Australian band released the 1987 album "Diesel and Dust"?
fact: It includes "Beds Are Burning", a protest song calling for Aboriginal land to be given back.

text: In the film "The Castle", the Kerrigan family home is in which Melbourne suburb?
fact: Bonnie Doon is where the Kerrigans have their holiday house.

text: Which yacht won the America's Cup for Australia in 1983?
fact: It ended the New York Yacht Club's 132-year hold on the Cup.

text: The children's TV show "Bluey" is set in which city?
fact: Its houses are modelled on Brisbane's high-set Queenslander homes.

text: Vegemite was created in 1922 using leftover yeast from what?
fact: Chemist Cyril Callister developed the recipe in Melbourne.

text: The lamington is named after Lord Lamington, governor of which colony?
fact: Lord Lamington was governor of Queensland from 1896 to 1901.

text: The word "kangaroo" comes from which Aboriginal language?
fact: Cook's crew recorded it in 1770 while repairing the Endeavour.

text: In 2021, the anthem line "For we are young and free" became "For we are ___ and free".
fact: The change took effect on 1 January 2021.

text: Platypuses and echidnas belong to which group of egg-laying mammals?
fact: Monotremes have no nipples. Milk seeps through patches of skin.

text: Wombats are famous for producing droppings of what shape?
Which snake has the most toxic venom of any land snake?
fact: It lives in remote country near the Queensland–South Australia border and is rarely seen.

text: Which bird appears on the Australian 10-cent coin?
fact: The coin shows a male superb lyrebird and was designed by Stuart Devlin.

text: Irukandji syndrome is caused by the sting of what kind of creature?
fact: The Irukandji jellyfish's bell is only about 1 to 3 cm across.

text: Cane toads were brought to Queensland in 1935 to control what?
fact: The toads did little to control the beetles and spread across the north instead.

text: What does the male platypus have on its hind legs?
fact: The venom causes severe pain in people that can last for months.

text: Which is the only Australian state with a single house of parliament?
fact: Queensland abolished its upper house in 1922.

text: How long is a state senator's normal term in the federal Senate?
fact: Half the state senators face election every three years.

text: Robert Menzies founded which political party in 1944–45?
fact: Menzies had led the United Australia Party, which the Liberals replaced.

text: What is the longest a federal House of Representatives can run before an election?
fact: The three years run from the House's first sitting, not from election day.

text: In Aussie slang, what is a "bingle"?
In Aussie slang, what is a "furphy"?
fact: It comes from carts made by the Furphy firm, seen in Australian army camps in WWI.

text: If an Aussie says "have a Captain Cook", what do they mean?
fact: It's rhyming slang: "Cook" rhymes with "look".

text: Someone "on the wallaby track" was doing what?
In Australian English, what is "the Never Never"?
fact: Jeannie Gunn's book "We of the Never Never" is set on Elsey Station in the NT.

text: If a pub is "chockers", what is it?
fact: It comes from "chock-a-block", a sailing term for pulley blocks hauled tight together.

text: What does it mean to "spit the dummy"?
fact: A "dummy" is the Australian word for a baby's pacifier.

text: What percentage of voters said Yes in the 1967 referendum on Aboriginal Australians?
fact: The exact figure was 90.77%, the highest Yes vote in any federal referendum.

text: In his final Test innings, how many runs did Don Bradman need to average exactly 100?
fact: He was out second ball for a duck and finished on 99.94.

text: How many players per team are on the field at once in an AFL match?
How long is the Melbourne Cup race?
fact: Before metric conversion in 1972 it was run over two miles.

text: In total, how many senators represent each state in the federal Senate?
fact: The territories get two senators each.

text: In what year did the last known captive thylacine die at Hobart Zoo?
fact: It died on 7 September, now marked as National Threatened Species Day.

text: In what year did Cyclone Tracy devastate Darwin on Christmas Day?
How many metres does Uluru rise above the surrounding plain?
fact: Like an iceberg, most of the rock is believed to be underground.

text: Roughly how long is the Great Barrier Reef?
fact: It's made of about 2900 separate reefs and 900 islands.

text: In what year did federal parliament pass the law making voting compulsory?
fact: Turnout jumped from under 60% to over 90% at the next election, in 1925.

text: How many ships made up the First Fleet?
fact: Six were convict transports, two were warships and three carried stores.

text: How tall is Mount Kosciuszko?
fact: Polish explorer Paul Strzelecki named it in 1840 after a Polish patriot.

text: In what year was the Eureka Stockade battle fought at Ballarat?
fact: The Eureka flag, with its Southern Cross, was flown there.

text: In what year was the first Melbourne Cup run?
fact: It was won by a horse called Archer.

text: Put these cities in order of their European founding, earliest first.
Put these prime ministers in order of first taking office, earliest first.
Put these events in Australian history in order, earliest first.
Put these in order of area, largest first.
Put these Australian cities in order from north to south, northernmost first.
Put these Australian films in order of release, earliest first.
Put these Australian TV shows in order of first airing, earliest first.
Put these conflicts in order of Australian troops first going, earliest first.
In Space Jam (1996), what is the name of the Looney Tunes team Michael Jordan plays for?
fact: The Monstars are the opposition. Joe Pytka directed the film.

text: Which NBA team plays its home games at Madison Square Garden?
fact: The team moved into the current Garden when it opened in 1968.

text: As of the end of the 2024-25 season, who had made the most three-pointers in NBA history?
fact: Curry took the record in December 2021.

text: The documentary series The Last Dance follows which team's 1997-98 season?
fact: The ten-part series was directed by Jason Hehir and released in 2020.

text: Which team came from 3-1 down to beat Golden State in the 2016 NBA Finals?
fact: No team had won the Finals from 3-1 down before. LeBron James was Finals MVP.

text: Which country does NBA star Luka Doncic come from?
fact: He was born in Ljubljana in 1999 and played for Real Madrid before the NBA.

text: What did James Naismith use as goals when he invented basketball?
fact: He had asked the janitor for boxes. The janitor came back with baskets instead.

text: What is Tasmania's NBL team, the 2024 champions, called?
fact: The jack jumper is a venomous ant common in Tasmania. The club joined the NBL in 2021.

text: Patty Mills won the 2014 NBA championship with which team?
fact: They beat Miami 4-1, sealing it with a 104-87 win in Game 5.

text: The NBA's championship trophy is named after which former commissioner?
fact: O'Brien ran the league from 1975 to 1984. The trophy took his name in 1984.

text: Which NBA team was the Seattle SuperSonics until 2008?
fact: The SuperSonics won their only NBA title in 1979, beating the Washington Bullets.

text: Which player is the silhouette in the NBA logo said to be based on?
fact: Designer Alan Siegel says he worked from a photo of West. The NBA long declined to confirm it.

text: Which team drafted Kobe Bryant in 1996, then traded him to the Lakers?
fact: He went 13th overall, and the Lakers gave up centre Vlade Divac to get him.

text: Which NBA award did Australian Dyson Daniels win for the 2024-25 season?
fact: He led the league with 229 steals and was runner-up for Defensive Player of the Year.

text: Lauren Jackson won two WNBA championships with which team?
fact: She was the first pick in the 2001 draft, and won titles in 2004 and 2010 and three MVPs.

text: Who was the first Australian to play in the NBA?
fact: Minnesota drafted him seventh in 1991. He later won three titles alongside Michael Jordan.

text: Whose three-pointer with 5.2 seconds left forced overtime in Game 6 of the 2013 NBA Finals?
fact: Miami trailed San Antonio 95-92. They won in overtime, then took the title in Game 7.

text: NBA star Kyrie Irving was born in which Australian city?
fact: His American father was playing for the Bulleen Boomers. The family left when he was two.

text: As of the end of the 2024-25 season, which club had won the most NBL championships?
fact: Perth's tenth title came in 2020. No other club had more than six.

text: Which university did Michael Jordan play for?
fact: As a freshman he hit the winning shot against Georgetown in the 1982 NCAA final.

text: In the NBA, a player is disqualified from the game on which personal foul?
fact: Under FIBA rules, used at the Olympics, a player is out after five.

text: Who was head coach of the Boomers at the 2024 Paris Olympics?
fact: Born in California, he also led them at the 2004, 2008 and Tokyo Games.

text: Which team was known as the "Bad Boys" when it won NBA titles in 1989 and 1990?
fact: Chuck Daly coached them. He went on to coach the original Dream Team.

text: Who was the only college player on the original US Olympic "Dream Team"?
fact: The Duke forward was picked ahead of Shaquille O'Neal.

text: Which 1998 Spike Lee film stars Denzel Washington as the father of a top basketball prospect?
fact: The son, Jesus Shuttlesworth, was played by a real NBA guard.

text: The Sacramento Kings franchise won the 1951 NBA title under what name?
fact: The franchise moved to Cincinnati in 1957, Kansas City in 1972 and Sacramento in 1985.

text: Who was the first Black player to appear in an NBA game, in October 1950?
fact: Lloyd played for the Washington Capitols on 31 October 1950, a day before Cooper's debut.

text: Which team retired Michael Jordan's number 23 even though he never played for it?
fact: Pat Riley led the ceremony in April 2003, before Jordan's last game in Miami.

text: Who recorded the NBA's first official quadruple-double, in 1974?
fact: He had 22 points, 14 rebounds, 13 assists and 12 blocks in an overtime win over Atlanta.

text: Which club won the first NBL championship, in 1979?
fact: They beat Canberra 94-93 in the final, and won again in 1980.

text: Which Opal was named MVP of the 2006 World Championship, which Australia won?
fact: The tournament was held in Brazil. Australia beat Russia 91-74 in the final.

text: Despite their name, the Harlem Globetrotters were founded in which city?
fact: They began on the South Side in 1926. Their theme tune is Sweet Georgia Brown.

text: Who won the 1984 NBA Slam Dunk Contest, beating Julius Erving in the final?
fact: Nance, of the Phoenix Suns, won after Erving missed one of his three dunks in the final.

text: Who "stole the ball" to save Boston in Game 7 of the 1965 Eastern finals, in a famous radio call?
fact: Johnny Most made the call. Havlicek tipped Hal Greer's inbound pass with five seconds left.

text: Larry Bird led which college to the 1979 NCAA final against Magic Johnson's Michigan State?
fact: Indiana State went in unbeaten at 33-0. Michigan State won 75-64.

text: Who handed out 30 assists in a game in December 1990, setting an NBA record?
fact: Skiles did it for Orlando against Denver, beating Kevin Porter's 29 from 1978.

text: How many seconds is the NBA shot clock?
fact: It was introduced in 1954, pushed by Syracuse Nationals owner Danny Biasone.

text: How many points did Wilt Chamberlain score in one NBA game in March 1962?
fact: His Philadelphia Warriors won 169-147 in Hershey, Pennsylvania. The game was not televised.

text: How many NBA championships did Bill Russell win as a player?
fact: All of them came with Boston in 13 seasons, the last two as player-coach.

text: In what year did James Naismith invent basketball?
fact: He wrote 13 rules for his class at a YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts.

text: How many Olympic Games did Andrew Gaze play in for the Boomers?
fact: He played at every Games from 1984 to 2000 and carried the flag in Sydney.

text: As of the end of 2024-25, the NBA's longest winning streak was the 1971-72 Lakers'. How many games?
fact: The run began in November 1971. Milwaukee ended it in January 1972.

text: With which pick in the 2014 NBA draft did Denver select Nikola Jokic?
fact: His selection ran on a ticker while the broadcast showed a Taco Bell ad.

text: In what year did the NBA adopt the three-point line?
fact: It came in for the 1979-80 season, borrowed from the old ABA.

text: How long is an NBA court, in feet?
fact: It is 50 feet wide. International courts are a little smaller, at 28 metres by 15.

text: Put these players in order of height, tallest first.
Put these Australians in order of the year they were drafted into the NBA, earliest first.
Put these in order of career NBA regular-season points at the end of 2024-25, most first.
Put these teams in order of NBA championships won as of the end of 2024-25, most first.
Put these teams in order of their first NBA season, earliest first.
Ryan Gosling and Christina Aguilera were child cast members of which TV show?
fact: Both joined the Disney Channel show in 1993, aged 12. Keri Russell was a castmate.

text: Before wrestling as The Rock, Dwayne Johnson played which sport for the University of Miami?
fact: He was in Miami's 1991 national championship team, then had a short stint in Canada.

text: Harrison Ford spent years between acting jobs working as what?
fact: He taught himself the trade. His clients included the writer Joan Didion.

text: Which mobile phone maker began in 1865 as a wood pulp mill?
fact: The mill was in Tampere, Finland. Rubber and cables came with a merger in 1967.

text: Before Twilight, Robert Pattinson played which Hogwarts student in a Harry Potter film?
fact: He appeared in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (2005).

text: What was Albert Einstein's day job in 1905, when he published his theory of special relativity?
fact: He worked at the Swiss Patent Office in Bern from 1902 to 1909.

text: Before his TV comedy career, Paul Hogan worked as a rigger on which landmark?
fact: His workmates on the bridge talked him into entering the TV talent show New Faces.

text: Selena Gomez and Demi Lovato were child actors together on which TV show?
fact: Both joined in 2002. Gomez played Gianna and Lovato played Angela.
wrong: Bear in the Big Blue House

text: As a teenager in the English village of Holmes Chapel, Harry Styles had a part-time job where?
fact: He mentioned his Saturday job at the W. Mandeville bakery in his first X Factor interview.
wrong: In a fish and chip shop

text: Which sport was Usain Bolt's first love as a boy, before a coach steered him to the track?
fact: He was a fast bowler as a boy, before his school coaches pointed him to athletics.

text: Which actor was a New York City firefighter from 1980 to 1984, before his film career took off?
fact: He served with Engine Company 55 in Manhattan, taking acting classes on the side.

text: Before The Police, Sting spent two years working as what?
fact: He taught at St Paul's First School in Cramlington, north of Newcastle upon Tyne.

text: Before acting, Jason Statham competed for England at the 1990 Commonwealth Games in which sport?
fact: The Games were in Auckland. His best finish was eighth, in the 1 metre springboard.

text: Agatha Christie picked up her knowledge of poisons during World War I while working where?
fact: She worked at the Red Cross hospital in Torquay and qualified as an apothecary's assistant.

text: Dev Patel, Daniel Kaluuya and Nicholas Hoult all had early roles in which British teen drama?
fact: It began on E4 in 2007. Kaluuya also wrote two of its episodes.

text: Tom Holland's first big role, from 2008 to 2010, was the lead in which West End musical?
fact: He was 12 when he took over the title role at the Victoria Palace Theatre in 2008.

text: Katy Perry's first album came out in 2001 under her real name, Katy Hudson. What kind of music was it?
fact: Her parents were both pastors. The record label went bankrupt months after the release.

text: Which actor joined the US Marines after the September 11 attacks, years before starring in Star Wars?
fact: He served for nearly three years, then studied acting at Juilliard in New York.

text: Sam Kerr played which sport until she was 12, when she switched to soccer?
fact: As a girl she dreamed of playing for the West Coast Eagles.

text: Which prime minister had driven steam trains for the NSW railways before entering politics?
fact: By 1914 he was a first-class engine driver in Bathurst, the youngest in the state.

text: Holden began in Adelaide in 1856 as a maker of what?
fact: James Alexander Holden's firm moved on to trimming carriages, then to building car bodies.

text: John Farnham was an apprentice in which trade when he recorded Sadie (The Cleaning Lady) in 1967?
fact: Sadie came out that November, went to No. 1 and sold about 180,000 copies.

text: The Musée d'Orsay in Paris is housed in a grand building that opened in 1900 as what?
fact: The Gare d'Orsay was finished in time for the 1900 world's fair. The museum opened in 1986.

text: Which actor rowed for Cambridge in the 1980 Boat Race, losing to Oxford by a few feet?
fact: Oxford won by a canvas. His father, Ran Laurie, won Olympic rowing gold in 1948.

text: Which future prime minister managed a rock band called The Ramrods in the 1960s?
fact: At the time he was also a researcher and advocate for a council workers' union.

text: After university, Margaret Thatcher worked for four years in which job before becoming a barrister?
fact: She studied chemistry at Oxford, then worked for a plastics firm and for J. Lyons and Co.

text: Pope Francis told parishioners in 2013 that he had once held which job in Buenos Aires?
fact: He also trained as a chemical technician and worked in the food industry.

text: Barack Obama's first job, as a teenager in Honolulu, was at a branch of which chain?
fact: He wrote in 2016 that scooping rock-hard ice cream was brutal on the wrists.

text: As a schoolboy in 1964, Phil Collins was an extra in which film?
fact: He was 13, in the crowd for the Beatles' TV concert. He also played the Artful Dodger on stage.

text: Flume first made music as a boy with software that came free with what?
fact: He spotted the promotion in a supermarket with his dad. The disc held a simple music program.

text: As pop singer Russ Le Roq, Russell Crowe released a 1982 single saying he wanted to be like whom?
fact: I Just Wanna Be Like Marlon Brando came out in New Zealand and was not a hit.

text: Before Canva, Melanie Perkins co-founded Fusion Books, which let schools design what online?
fact: She started it in Perth with Cliff Obrecht, who went on to co-found Canva with her.

text: What stood on Bennelong Point until 1958, when it was knocked down to make way for the Opera House?
fact: Fort Macquarie Tram Depot, opened in 1902, was built to look like a castle.

text: Banjo Paterson wrote Clancy of the Overflow and The Man from Snowy River while working as what?
fact: He was admitted as a solicitor in 1886 and practised in Sydney for more than a decade.

text: Before turning to comedy full time, Shaun Micallef spent ten years working as what?
fact: He studied law at the University of Adelaide, where he performed in comedy revues.

text: Before he took up karting, Oscar Piastri was a national champion at nine, racing what?
fact: He has said he won the second class at the nationals. He started karting at 10.

text: How old was Billie Eilish when she uploaded Ocean Eyes to SoundCloud in November 2015?
fact: Her brother Finneas wrote the song. She turned 14 a month later.

text: Comedian Volodymyr Zelenskyy played Ukraine's president in a TV sitcom. In what year was he elected for real?
fact: The sitcom, Servant of the People, began in 2015. His party took the same name.

text: In what year did Jeff Bezos's Amazon open for business, as an online bookshop?
fact: The site went live that July. The company had been founded a year earlier as Cadabra.

text: How many times did Arnold Schwarzenegger win bodybuilding's Mr Olympia title?
fact: He won six in a row from 1970 to 1975, then came back to win again in 1980.

text: Harrison Ford was a jobbing actor for years. How old was he when Star Wars came out in May 1977?
fact: He was born in July 1942. George Lucas had first cast him in American Graffiti (1973).

text: In what year was Netflix founded, as a company that rented out DVDs by post?
fact: Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph started it in California. Streaming followed in 2007.

text: In what year was Samsung founded, as a small trading company dealing in dried fish and noodles?
fact: Lee Byung-chul started it with 40 staff. It moved into electronics in the late 1960s.

text: Alan Rickman made his film debut as Hans Gruber in Die Hard (1988). How old was he at its release?
fact: Born in February 1946, he had made his name on stage with the Royal Shakespeare Company.

text: Brian May put his astrophysics doctorate on hold for Queen. In what year did he finally complete it?
fact: He handed in his thesis, on dust in the solar system, at Imperial College London that August.

In Cluedo, what rank does the suspect Mustard hold?
fact: He is one of six suspects, along with Miss Scarlett and Professor Plum.

text: Which chess piece moves in an L shape and can jump over other pieces?
fact: Each player starts with two of them.

text: Which four colours make up a classic Uno deck?
fact: Merle Robbins devised Uno in Ohio in 1971.

text: In Monopoly, what happens when you roll doubles three times in a row?
fact: Landing on Go to Jail, or drawing the wrong card, will also send you there.

text: In the game Operation, which part of the patient lights up when you touch the sides?
fact: The patient is called Cavity Sam, and a buzzer goes off as well.

text: In Twister, what decides which hand or foot goes on which colour?
fact: The mat has 24 circles, in four rows of six.

text: In Dungeons & Dragons, what is the player who runs the game and tells the story called?
fact: The job, part referee and part storyteller, is usually shortened to DM.

text: In Cards Against Humanity, what colour are the question cards?
fact: The game was funded on Kickstarter and came out in 2011.

text: How many dice are rolled in Yahtzee?
fact: All five showing the same number is a Yahtzee, worth 50 points.

text: In English-language Scrabble, which two letters are worth 10 points each?
fact: J and X are worth 8 each. There is only one tile of each of the four letters.

text: Which of these is one of the four stations on the London Monopoly board?
fact: The other three are King's Cross, Fenchurch Street and Liverpool Street.

text: Trivial Pursuit was created in 1979 by Chris Haney and Scott Abbott in which country?
fact: The two journalists thought of it in Montreal, and it went on sale in 1981.

text: In Catan, rolling which total on the two dice lets you move the robber?
fact: Nobody collects resources, and anyone holding more than seven cards loses half of them.

text: The word "meeple" was first used for the little wooden followers in which game?
fact: Alison Hansel is credited with running "my people" together during a game.

text: In Codenames, picking which card makes your team lose on the spot?
fact: The 25 word cards are laid out in a five by five grid.

text: In Pandemic, in which city do all the players start the game?
fact: The first research station goes there too. It is the home of America's real CDC.

text: In classic Risk, which of these is one of the four territories of Australia?
fact: The others are New Guinea, Western Australia and Eastern Australia. Siam is in Asia.

text: The Australian board game Squatter, launched in 1962, has players running what?
fact: Bob Lloyd launched it at the Royal Melbourne Show.

text: In Texas hold 'em, what is the fifth and last community card called?
fact: The first three cards are the flop and the fourth is the turn.

text: Which of these is one of the three suits in mahjong?
fact: The other two suits are circles and characters.

text: Snakes and ladders began as a game of moral lessons in which country?
fact: The ladders stood for virtues and the snakes for vices.

text: Magic: The Gathering has five colours of mana: white, blue, black, red and which other?
fact: Richard Garfield created the game, which first went on sale in 1993.

text: Which company's first game, in 1860, was The Checkered Game of Life?
fact: The modern Game of Life followed a century later, in 1960.

text: What is the highest number on a standard backgammon doubling cube?
fact: Its six faces read 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64.

text: Monopoly grew out of The Landlord's Game. Who patented that game in 1904?
fact: Charles Darrow later sold his version of the game to Parker Brothers.

text: Cluedo's victim was long called Dr Black. What was he called in Clue, the North American version?
fact: Since 2023 both versions have shared one merged name, with "Boddy" as his nickname.

text: Albert Lamorisse, the Frenchman who invented Risk, was best known for what?
fact: His short film The Red Balloon won an Oscar. Risk first came out in France in 1957.

text: Who designed the railway board game Ticket to Ride?
fact: It won Germany's Spiel des Jahres, the Game of the Year award, in 2004.

text: Wingspan's Oceania expansion, full of Australian birds, added which new kind of food?
fact: The expansion also covers the birds of New Zealand.

text: Which Go champion lost 4-1 to Google DeepMind's AlphaGo in Seoul in 2016?
fact: Lee won the fourth game. Fan Hui had lost 5-0 in 2015, and Ke Jie lost 3-0 in 2017.

text: Mahjong has three dragon tiles: red, green and which other colour?
fact: The white dragon is often a tile with nothing on its face.

text: The joker joined the pack in 19th-century America as the top trump in which card game?
fact: An 1860s version of the card was labelled the Imperial Bower.

text: In the standard English pattern of playing cards, which king is drawn in profile, with one eye?
fact: The jacks of spades and hearts are in profile too: the one-eyed jacks.

text: In two-up, what is the flat piece of wood that the coins are tossed from called?
fact: The boxer runs the game, the ringie looks after the ring and the cockatoo kept watch for police.

text: The Royal Game of Ur, about 4,500 years old, is named after a city in which modern country?
fact: Leonard Woolley found five boards in the Royal Cemetery at Ur. One is in the British Museum.

text: Which German city hosts Spiel, the huge board game fair that began in 1983?
fact: It is held in October and calls itself the world's largest public fair for board games.

text: How many pieces does each player have at the start of a game of chess?
fact: Eight pawns, two rooks, two knights, two bishops, a queen and a king.

text: In blackjack, what total are players trying to get close to without going over?
fact: An ace with a ten-value card is a natural, which beats a 21 made from three or more cards.

text: In draughts on a standard 8 by 8 board, how many pieces does each player start with?
fact: A piece that reaches the far row is crowned a king and can then move backwards too.

text: How many tiles are in a standard double-six set of dominoes?
fact: A double-nine set has 55.

text: In what year did IBM's Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov in a six-game chess match?
fact: Kasparov had won their first match 4-2 the year before. The rematch finished 3.5 to 2.5.

text: In what year was Dungeons & Dragons first published?
fact: It was created by Gary Gygax and Dave Arneson and published by TSR.

text: How many wooden blocks are in a classic Jenga set?
fact: They are stacked three to a layer in a tower 18 layers high.

text: A full-size Go board is a grid of how many lines in each direction?
fact: Stones go on the points where lines cross, and there are 361 of them.

text: In the Pokémon Trading Card Game, how many cards must a player's deck contain?
fact: Each player sets six of them aside as Prize cards at the start.

text: Put these players in the order they first became world chess champion, earliest first.
The Superbank, a long sand-bottom wave that starts at Snapper Rocks, is in which city?
In board sports, what does it mean to ride "goofy"?
fact: Left foot forward is known as regular.

text: In the film Point Break, the bank-robbing surfers hide behind masks of whom?
fact: The gang, the Ex-Presidents, wear Reagan, Carter, Nixon and Johnson masks.

text: The surfing at the Paris 2024 Olympics was held at Teahupo'o, on which island?
fact: The reef there lies so close to the surface that the wave breaks thick and hollow.

text: What is skateboarder Tony Hawk's nickname?
Which skate shoe brand began in 1966 as a factory and shop in Anaheim, California?
fact: It opened as the Van Doren Rubber Company, making shoes on site and selling them direct.

text: Which American snowboarder was nicknamed "the Flying Tomato" for his red hair?
Which Australian won snowboard halfpipe silver at both the 2022 and 2026 Winter Olympics?
fact: He also won bronze in 2018, when he carried the flag at the opening ceremony.

text: Stephanie Gilmore won a record eighth women's world title in 2022 by beating which Hawaiian in the final?
fact: Gilmore began the finals day as fifth seed and won every heat.

text: As of the end of 2025, who is the only surfer to have won six world titles in a row?
fact: Kelly Slater's longest streak is five.

text: Rip Curl and Quiksilver were both founded in which Victorian surf town?
fact: Rip Curl started out making surfboards, then turned to wetsuits.

text: Which Australian won the 2025 women's world surfing title at Cloudbreak in Fiji?
fact: She beat American Caroline Marks in a best-of-three title match.

text: Duke Kahanamoku gave his first Australian surfboard display, in the summer of 1914-15, at which Sydney beach?
fact: The Hawaiian swimming champion shaped the board himself from sugar pine. The surf club still has it.

text: Puberty Blues, the 1979 novel filmed in 1981, is set among the surfers of which Sydney beach suburb?
fact: Kathy Lette and Gabrielle Carey wrote the novel. Bruce Beresford directed the film.

text: The Eddie, a big-wave contest held only when the surf is huge, takes place at which Hawaiian bay?
fact: Named for lifeguard Eddie Aikau, it needs wave faces of 30 to 40 feet to run.

text: Which freestyle skater invented the modern kickflip in the early 1980s, a trick soon dubbed the "magic flip"?
fact: He also took the ollie from ramps to flat ground, which opened the way for street skating.

text: Keegan Palmer won gold for Australia at both Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024 in which event?
fact: He was born in San Diego and moved to Queensland as a young child.

text: In May 2024, Australia's Arisa Trew became the first female skateboarder to land which spin?
fact: That is two and a half turns. A year earlier she was the first woman to land a 720 in a contest.

text: Which skater and MTV host founded Street League Skateboarding in 2010?
fact: He made his name on TV with Rob & Big, Fantasy Factory and Ridiculousness.

text: In 2005, skateboarder Danny Way used a giant ramp to jump over which landmark?
fact: He cleared a gap of more than 18 metres with no motor to help.

text: Which future federal MP won Australia's first Winter Olympic skiing medal, a slalom bronze in 1998?
fact: She won the seat of Warringah from former prime minister Tony Abbott in 2019.

text: The Skitube, a rack railway running mostly through tunnels, carries skiers up to which resort?
fact: It climbs from Bullocks Flat on the Alpine Way and runs on to Blue Cow.

text: What do skiers and snowboarders mean by "corduroy"?
fact: Grooming machines leave neat ridges that look like the fabric.

text: Who in 1976 became the first professional world surfing champion?
fact: The tour began that year as International Professional Surfers, or IPS.

text: Which Australian surfer and shaper invented the three-fin "thruster" at the start of the 1980s?
fact: He won at Bells Beach and Pipeline on it in 1981, and it became the standard design.

text: Who was the first goofy-footer to win surfing's men's professional world title?
fact: He won two world titles in a row and the Pipe Masters three times.

text: The ollie takes its name from the nickname of which Florida skater, who invented it in the 1970s?
fact: A friend, Scott Goodman, gave him the nickname.

text: The first X Games, in 1995, were based in which US state?
fact: That year they were called the Extreme Games. The shorter name came in 1996.

text: Which European country outlawed skateboards from the late 1970s until 1989?
fact: With boards banned from sale and use, skaters built ramps hidden in the woods.

text: The Z-Boys, the 1970s skaters of Dogtown on the Los Angeles coast, took their name from what?
fact: Tony Alva, Jay Adams and Stacy Peralta all rode for the team.

text: Which studio developed the first Tony Hawk's Pro Skater, released in 1999?
fact: In Australia the game was sold as Tony Hawk's Skateboarding.

text: Who won the first Olympic snowboarding gold medal, in the giant slalom at Nagano 1998?
fact: Snowboarding made its Olympic debut at those Games, with giant slalom and halfpipe.

text: Which Japanese Olympic halfpipe champion also skateboarded at the Tokyo 2020 Games?
fact: He came 14th on a skateboard, then won snowboard gold six months later in Beijing.

text: The Streif, the most feared downhill course in World Cup skiing, is in which Austrian town?
fact: It runs down the Hahnenkamm, the mountain that gives the race its name.

text: The Kangaroo Hoppet, a 42 km cross-country ski race, is held each August at which resort?
fact: It is Australia's leg of the Worldloppet series of ski marathons.

text: Which toy, invented in Michigan in 1965, is seen as the forerunner of the snowboard?
fact: Sherman Poppen made it for his children. His wife named it, from "snow" and "surfer".

text: As of the end of 2025, how many world surfing titles had Kelly Slater won?
fact: He won his first at 20 and his eleventh at 39.

text: How many Olympic gold medals did snowboarder Shaun White win?
fact: All three came in the halfpipe, in 2006, 2010 and 2018.

text: In what year did Tony Hawk land the first 900, at the X Games in San Francisco?
fact: The clock had run out, but he was allowed to keep trying until he landed it.

text: In what year did Torah Bright win Olympic gold in the snowboard halfpipe?
fact: She won in Vancouver, then took silver in Sochi four years later.

text: How old was Chloe Kim when she won her first Olympic halfpipe gold, at PyeongChang in 2018?
fact: She won again in 2022 and took silver in 2026.

text: How old was Kelly Slater when he won the Pipeline Pro in February 2022?
fact: He turned 50 six days later. His first win at Pipeline had come 30 years earlier.

text: In what year was the Surf Bathing Association of NSW, now Surf Life Saving Australia, founded?
fact: Sydney's surf clubs formed it that October.

text: In what year was the skateboarding magazine Thrasher first published?
fact: It was launched in San Francisco, mainly to promote Independent skateboard trucks.

text: In what year did Jake Burton Carpenter found Burton Snowboards in Vermont?
fact: He started out building boards in a barn.

What does DNA stand for?
fact: The human genome holds about 3 billion DNA base pairs.

text: What is the hardest substance in the human body?
fact: Enamel is about 96 per cent mineral, but once it wears away the body cannot regrow it.

text: What is the largest artery in the human body?
fact: It carries oxygen-rich blood out of the heart to the rest of the body.

text: Florence Nightingale became famous for nursing British soldiers in which war?
fact: She reached the army hospital at Scutari in November 1854 with a party of 38 nurses.

text: What is the medical name for the collarbone?
fact: The name comes from the Latin for "little key".

text: Which tiny cell fragments in the blood clump together to plug a cut?
fact: They are made in the bone marrow and last only about seven to ten days.

text: The sleep stage with the most vivid dreams is called REM sleep. What does REM stand for?
fact: It was first described in the 1950s. Adults spend about a quarter of their sleep in it.

text: Hair and fingernails are made mainly of which protein?
fact: The same protein makes horns, hooves, wool and feathers.

text: Which acid does your stomach make to help break down food?
fact: Cells in the stomach lining make it, keeping the inside at a pH of roughly 2.

text: What do you actually hit when you bang your "funny bone"?
fact: It is the ulnar nerve, which runs close under the skin at the elbow.
wrong: The tip of the arm bone

text: What is the name of the topmost bone of the spine, which holds up the skull?
fact: It is named after the Titan of Greek myth who held up the sky.

text: The hippocampus, a part of the brain vital to memory, is named after which sea creature?
fact: The name is Greek: hippos means horse and kampos means sea monster.

text: On average, which is the heaviest organ inside an adult's body?
fact: It weighs about 1.5 kg, a little more than the brain.

text: Blood types are Rh positive or Rh negative. The "Rh" comes from the name of which animal?
fact: The name stuck, though the human factor later proved to differ from the one in the monkeys.

text: Which surgeon pioneered antiseptic surgery in the 1860s, using carbolic acid to kill germs?
fact: Listerine mouthwash was named in his honour in 1879.

text: Eye surgeon Fred Hollows, famed for restoring sight to thousands, was born in which country?
fact: He was born in Dunedin in 1929. The Fred Hollows Foundation was set up in 1992.

text: Which lobe of the brain does most of the work of processing what you see?
fact: It sits at the very back of the head.

text: What makes the popping sound when you crack your knuckles?
fact: The same knuckle will not crack again straight away. It needs time to reset first.
answer: Gas bubbles in the joint fluid

text: What colour is the oxygen-poor blood in the veins of your arm?
fact: Veins only look blue because of the way skin scatters and absorbs light.

text: Which cells in the retina let you see colour?
fact: Rods take over in dim light, which is why colours fade at night.

text: Perth surgeon Fiona Wood, the 2005 Australian of the Year, is best known for developing what?
fact: She developed it with scientist Marie Stoner. It is now sold as ReCell.

text: Which hormone, released by the pineal gland as night falls, helps set your sleep cycle?
fact: Its level in the blood is low by day and high at night.

text: Hiccups are caused by sudden spasms of which muscle?
fact: Each spasm snaps the vocal cords shut, which makes the "hic" sound.

text: Which U-shaped bone is joined to no other bone, held in place only by muscles and ligaments?
fact: It sits in the front of the neck, below the jaw, and is sometimes called the floating bone.

text: Which is the longest muscle in the human body?
fact: It runs from the hip to the inner knee. Its name comes from the Latin for tailor.

text: The coccyx, or tailbone, takes its name from the Greek word for which bird?
fact: Seen from the side, the bone was thought to look like the bird's beak.

text: Where on the body is the glabella?
fact: The name comes from the Latin for smooth or hairless.
wrong: Between the nose and top lip
At the back of the knee
At the base of the thumb

text: Broca's area, in the left frontal lobe of the brain, is most closely linked with what?
fact: French doctor Paul Broca described it in 1861.

text: What is the everyday name for sphenopalatine ganglioneuralgia?
fact: Pressing your tongue to the roof of your mouth can help it pass.

text: What happens when the tiny arrector pili muscles in your skin contract?
fact: In furry animals the same muscles fluff up the coat to trap warm air.

text: Which hormone, made mainly in the stomach, is nicknamed the "hunger hormone"?
fact: It signals the brain when the stomach is empty and it is time to eat.

text: The word "placebo" is Latin for what?
fact: Its opposite, the nocebo, takes its name from the Latin for "I shall harm".

text: Which anatomist published the landmark illustrated book De humani corporis fabrica in 1543?
fact: Based on his own dissections, it overturned ideas handed down from Galen.

text: Who in 1890 became the first woman registered as a doctor in Australia?
fact: Barred from studying medicine in Melbourne, she trained in the United States and Canada.

text: In the 1920s, Sydney doctor Mark Lidwill and physicist Edgar Booth built an early version of what?
fact: In 1932 New York doctor Albert Hyman called his own machine an "artificial pacemaker".

text: Hobart-born Elizabeth Blackburn shared a 2009 Nobel Prize for work on which part of a chromosome?
fact: They are protective caps on the ends of chromosomes, and they shorten as cells divide.

text: How many pairs of ribs do most people have?
fact: The bottom two pairs are called floating ribs because they join only the spine.

text: A popular myth says swallowed chewing gum stays in your stomach for how many years?
fact: Gum cannot be digested, but it passes through the gut and out like other food.

text: How many milk teeth, or baby teeth, are in a child's full set?
fact: They are usually all through by about the age of three.

text: In what year did the World Health Organization declare smallpox wiped out worldwide?
fact: The last natural case was in Somalia in October 1977.

text: In what year was the Human Genome Project declared complete?
fact: It covered about 92 per cent of the genome. The last gaps were filled in 2022.

text: How many bones are in one human hand, counting the wrist?
fact: Eight in the wrist, five in the palm and 14 in the fingers and thumb.

text: How many pairs of spinal nerves branch off the human spinal cord?
fact: Eight pairs in the neck, 12 in the chest, five lumbar, five sacral and one at the tailbone.

text: In what year was the textbook Gray's Anatomy first published?
fact: Henry Gray wrote the text and Henry Vandyke Carter drew the illustrations.

text: Human hearing is usually said to run from 20 hertz up to about how many hertz?
fact: The upper limit falls with age, and the slide starts in childhood.

In To Kill a Mockingbird, what is Atticus Finch's job?
fact: Harper Lee's novel won the 1961 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction.

text: In The Great Gatsby, what colour is the light at the end of Daisy's dock?
fact: Gatsby stares at it across the bay from the lawn of his mansion.

text: Which author created Robert Langdon, the hero of The Da Vinci Code?
fact: Langdon first appeared in Angels & Demons, published in 2000.

text: Which novel, set in Nazi Germany, is narrated by Death?
fact: Markus Zusak's narrator follows a girl called Liesel Meminger.
wrong: The Boy in the Striped Pyjamas
All the Light We Cannot See

text: Which Liane Moriarty novel became an HBO series with Nicole Kidman and Reese Witherspoon?
fact: The book is set on Sydney's Northern Beaches. The series moved the story to California.

text: Which Colleen Hoover novel, a BookTok favourite, became a 2024 film with Blake Lively?
fact: It came out in 2016 and found a huge new readership through TikTok in 2021.

text: In George Orwell's Animal Farm, what kind of animal is Napoleon, who seizes power?
fact: Boxer is the hard-working horse and Benjamin is the donkey.

text: Which former First Lady of the United States wrote the 2018 memoir Becoming?
In Roald Dahl's Matilda, who is the terrifying headmistress of Crunchem Hall?
fact: Pam Ferris played her in the 1996 film and Emma Thompson in the 2022 musical film.

text: Which novel opens: "Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way"?
fact: The wording is Constance Garnett's translation. Tolstoy's novel came out as a book in 1878.

text: Which Dickens novel ends: "it is a far, far better rest that I go to than I have ever known"?
fact: Its first line is just as famous: "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times".

text: In Steinbeck's Of Mice and Men, which animals does Lennie dream of tending on the farm he and George want?
fact: The title comes from Robert Burns's poem To a Mouse.

text: Who is the teenage narrator of J. D. Salinger's The Catcher in the Rye?
fact: Holden has just been expelled from his boarding school, Pencey Prep.

text: Haruki Murakami's novel Norwegian Wood takes its title from a song by which band?
fact: The narrator, Toru, hears the song as his plane lands in Hamburg.

text: Which Kazuo Ishiguro novel is narrated by Stevens, an English butler?
fact: It won the Booker Prize in 1989.

text: Which 2015 novel follows four friends, Jude, Willem, JB and Malcolm, in New York?
fact: Hanya Yanagihara's novel was shortlisted for the 2015 Booker Prize.

text: In Gillian Flynn's Gone Girl, Amy Dunne goes missing on which wedding anniversary?
fact: The novel came out in 2012. Rosamund Pike played Amy in the 2014 film.

text: In John Green's The Fault in Our Stars, Hazel and Augustus fly to which city to meet an author?
fact: The author, Peter Van Houten, wrote Hazel's favourite novel, An Imperial Affliction.

text: Who wrote the 1992 young adult novel Looking for Alibrandi?
fact: Pia Miranda played Josie Alibrandi in the 2000 film.

text: In Henry Lawson's story The Drover's Wife, what does the wife sit up all night watching for?
fact: It first appeared in The Bulletin in 1892. The family dog is called Alligator.

text: Anne Frank wrote her diary as letters to an imaginary friend. What did she call her?
fact: The diary was a present for her 13th birthday, in June 1942.

text: Schindler's List is based on a Booker Prize winner by which Australian author?
fact: The book, Schindler's Ark, won the Booker in 1982.

text: Which poet wrote "Do not go gentle into that good night"?
fact: The Welsh poet published it in 1951. It is a villanelle, built on two repeating lines.

text: In 2008, which Australian city was named a UNESCO City of Literature?
fact: Edinburgh was the first, in 2004. Hobart became Australia's second City of Literature in 2023.

text: In Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment, what is the surname of the former student at its centre?
fact: The novel is set in St Petersburg and first appeared in 1866.

text: Margaret Atwood shared the 2019 Booker Prize with which author?
fact: Atwood won for The Testaments, Evaristo for Girl, Woman, Other. The rules allowed one winner.

text: One Hundred Years of Solitude follows the Buendía family in which fictional town?
fact: Gabriel García Márquez's novel was first published in 1967.

text: Donna Tartt's The Goldfinch is named after a 1654 painting by which Dutch artist?
fact: Fabritius was a pupil of Rembrandt. Tartt's novel won the 2014 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction.

text: What does the original Swedish title of The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo mean in English?
fact: Stieg Larsson died in 2004. The novel was published in Sweden the following year.
wrong: The Girl Who Played with Fire

text: R. L. Stine's Goosebumps series began in 1992 with which book?
fact: The original series ran to 62 books between 1992 and 1997.

text: Banjo Paterson signed his early verse "The Banjo". Where did he get the name?
fact: His first poem appeared in The Bulletin in 1885, while he was studying law.

text: Who won the Miles Franklin Award for Carpentaria in 2007 and for Praiseworthy in 2024?
fact: Praiseworthy also won the 2024 Stella Prize, a prize she was the first to win twice.

text: Under which shared surname did the Brontë sisters first publish their work?
fact: They became Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell, each keeping her own initials.

text: On the first Penguin paperbacks, orange covers meant fiction. Which colour meant crime?
fact: Allen Lane launched Penguin in 1935, at sixpence a book. Dark blue was for biography.

text: In 1970 Penguin Australia defied the censors by secretly printing which banned novel?
fact: Philip Roth's novel was a prohibited import, so Penguin had it printed in Sydney.

text: Tina Fey based the film Mean Girls on which non-fiction book for parents?
fact: Rosalind Wiseman's book about teenage cliques came out in 2002.

text: In Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, how many Bennet sisters are there?
fact: Jane is the eldest and Lydia the youngest. Elizabeth comes second.

text: In what year was Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone first published?
fact: Bloomsbury's first hardback print run was just 500 copies.

text: Since 2007, how many digits are there in an ISBN, the number that identifies a book?
fact: Until the end of 2006 an ISBN had 10 digits.

text: In what year did Amazon release its first Kindle e-reader?
fact: It went on sale in the United States on 19 November that year.

text: How many novels are in John Marsden's Tomorrow series, not counting The Ellie Chronicles?
fact: The last, The Other Side of Dawn, came out in 1999.

text: In what year was the Booker Prize first awarded?
fact: The first winner was P. H. Newby, for Something to Answer For.

text: Patrick White's Voss was the first novel to win the Miles Franklin Award. In what year was it published?
fact: Miles Franklin died in 1954 and left her estate to found the prize.

text: In what year did Agatha Christie vanish for 11 days, setting off a nationwide search?
fact: She was found at a hotel in Harrogate, Yorkshire, booked in under another name.

text: Conan Doyle wrote 56 Sherlock Holmes short stories. How many Holmes novels did he write?
fact: A Study in Scarlet, The Sign of the Four, The Hound of the Baskervilles and The Valley of Fear.

Which sportswear brand's ads end with the slogan "Just Do It"?
fact: The line came from Dan Wieden of the ad agency Wieden+Kennedy.

text: Louie the Fly is the cartoon villain in ads for which insect spray?
fact: Jimmy White wrote Louie's gravelly jingle. The ads ran for more than half a century.

text: Which airline's ads have featured children's choirs singing I Still Call Australia Home?
fact: Peter Allen wrote the song in 1980.

text: Aleksandr Orlov, whose catchphrase is "Simples!", is what kind of animal?
fact: He fronts the ads for Compare the Market, with his sidekick Sergei.

text: In Australia, Snap, Crackle and Pop are the mascots of which Kellogg's cereal?
fact: Outside Australia and New Zealand the cereal is called Rice Krispies.

text: "Lowest prices are just the beginning" was the long-time slogan of which hardware chain?
fact: Bunnings dropped the line from its Australian ads and signs in 2020.

text: What kind of bird sits on a perch eating a cracker in the Arnott's logo?
fact: Arnott's dates its parrot emblem to 1888.

text: According to its slogan, which energy drink "gives you wings"?
fact: The brand itself spells the last word with three i's: "wiiings".

text: Which American rapper took over Menulog's "Did somebody say" jingle in 2020?
fact: Katy Perry sang her own version in 2022. Menulog closed in Australia in November 2025.

text: The line "Not happy, Jan!" comes from a TV ad for which business?
fact: Deborah Kennedy shouts it at Jan, who forgot to book the firm's ad in the directory.

text: "Jet Ski" is not a general word but a brand name. Which Japanese company owns it?
fact: Kawasaki's first stand-up Jet Ski models appeared in the early 1970s.

text: Who directed Apple's "1984" commercial, which launched the Macintosh during the Super Bowl?
fact: Made by the agency Chiat/Day, it had its only national airing on 22 January 1984.

text: Carlton Draught's "Big Ad" set new words to which piece of classical music?
fact: It comes from Carl Orff's Carmina Burana. The ad was shot near Queenstown, New Zealand.

text: Which former VFL footballer began fronting Australia Day lamb ads in 2005?
fact: He played 124 games for North Melbourne and became known as the "Lambassador".

text: In 2009 Kraft gave a new cheesy Vegemite spread which name, then dropped it within days?
fact: The name was unveiled during the AFL Grand Final. The spread became Cheesybite instead.

text: In E.T. (1982), which sweets lure the alien out, after Mars said no to using M&M's?
fact: Hershey said yes, and sales of the sweets leapt after the film came out.

text: Which shape hides in the white space between the E and the x of the FedEx logo?
fact: Lindon Leader of Landor Associates designed the logo.

text: Coles's "Down Down, prices are down" jingle reworked a hit by which British band?
fact: Coles launched its Down Down price campaign in 2010.

text: Which pop star recorded the song I'm Lovin' It when McDonald's launched the slogan in 2003?
fact: A German agency created the campaign, which began in Munich as "ich liebe es".

text: Which model asks "So where the bloody hell are you?" in Tourism Australia's 2006 ad?
fact: M&C Saatchi made the ad. Britain's TV ad clearance body objected to the word "bloody".

text: In Cadbury's famous ad, a gorilla plays the drums along to which song?
fact: The Phil Collins song sold Dairy Milk. Fallon London made the ad.

text: Which artist designed the Chupa Chups logo in 1969?
fact: Chupa Chups is a Spanish brand. Its name comes from chupar, "to suck".

text: How was Australia's Woolworths, founded in Sydney, linked to America's F. W. Woolworth chain?
fact: Its founders found the name was free to register in New South Wales.
wrong: It was the US firm's subsidiary

text: What do the I and K at the start of IKEA stand for?
fact: He was Ingvar Kamprad. E and A are Elmtaryd, his family's farm, and Agunnaryd, his village.

text: Which future blockbuster director made the first "Got Milk?" TV ad, in 1993?
fact: A history buff with a mouthful of peanut butter cannot say "Aaron Burr" to win a radio quiz.

text: Who played "the man your man could smell like" in Old Spice's ads?
fact: Terry Crews fronted a different run of Old Spice ads. The two shared a screen in 2015.

text: ASICS takes its name from a Latin phrase. What does the phrase mean?
fact: The Latin is anima sana in corpore sano. The firm began as Onitsuka in Kobe in 1949.
answer: A sound mind in a sound body

text: Häagen-Dazs, a made-up name meant to sound Danish, was founded in 1960 in which city?
fact: Reuben and Rose Mattus began it in the Bronx. The words mean nothing in any language.

text: Coca-Cola's contour bottle of 1915 was modelled on a picture of which plant's pod?
fact: Designers at the Root Glass Company of Indiana found the picture in a library.

text: Tiffany's trade mark blue has the Pantone number 1837. What does the number mark?
fact: The colour was on the cover of Tiffany's Blue Book catalogue by 1845.

text: The Esky, now a word Australians use for any cooler, was first made in Sydney by which firm?
fact: The first portable Esky went on sale in 1952.

text: Aspirin and Heroin both began in the 1890s as trade marks of which German company?
fact: Bayer sold Heroin as a cough remedy from 1898. Its Aspirin trade mark followed in 1899.

text: Which actor was the famous voice of VB's "hard earned thirst" ads?
fact: He played Walter Reilly in Crocodile Dundee. The ads kept using his voice after he died in 1989.

text: Holden's "Football, meat pies, kangaroos and Holden cars" jingle copied a US ad for which make?
fact: The American line ran "Baseball, hot dogs, apple pie and Chevrolet".

text: ABC's ad show Gruen is named after Victor Gruen, an architect famous for designing what?
fact: The "Gruen transfer" is the moment a confusing layout makes shoppers forget their plans.

text: Freddo Frog was created in 1930 at which Melbourne chocolate maker, bought by Cadbury in 1967?
fact: Harry Melbourne talked his bosses out of a chocolate mouse, saying it would scare children.

text: How many stripes make up the famous Adidas trade mark?
fact: Adi Dassler registered a shoe with the three stripes in 1949, the year he founded Adidas.

text: In what year did Coon cheese go back on sale under the new name Cheer?
fact: The new name was announced in January and the change was made in July.

text: In what year did Domino's unveil the logo that dropped the word "Pizza" from its name?
fact: The three dots on its logo stood for the three shops it had in 1965.

text: Coca-Cola's "Share a Coke" campaign, with names on the bottles, began in Australia in what year?
fact: The name sat on one side of the bottle, where the Coca-Cola logo used to be.

text: In what year did Bega Cheese buy Vegemite, bringing it back into Australian ownership?
fact: The seller was the American company Mondelez, formerly Kraft Foods.

text: In what year did Kentucky Fried Chicken officially adopt the name KFC?
fact: People had already been calling it KFC for years.

text: How many US dollars was student Carolyn Davidson paid in 1971 for designing the Nike swoosh?
fact: In 1983 Phil Knight gave her a gold swoosh ring and 500 Nike shares.

text: In what year did Coca-Cola launch New Coke, only to bring back the old recipe within three months?
fact: New Coke arrived on 23 April. The return of the original was announced on 11 July.

text: In what year did 7-Eleven take its name, from its new opening hours of 7 am to 11 pm?
fact: Before that the shops were called Tote'm Stores.

fact: Copywriter Frances Gerety wrote A Diamond Is Forever for De Beers.

text: Hyundai and Kia both come from which country?
fact: Hyundai bought a controlling stake in Kia in 1998.

text: Which car maker's badge is four linked rings?
fact: The rings stand for the four firms that formed Auto Union in 1932.

text: In a manual car, what does pressing the clutch pedal do?
Herbie, the star of The Love Bug, is what kind of car?
fact: Herbie is a 1963 model and wears the racing number 53.

text: Which company makes the Model 3 and the Model Y?
At the bowser, what do the numbers 91, 95 and 98 on petrol refer to?
fact: The higher the number, the more squeezing the fuel can take before it ignites by itself.

text: ABS helps a driver in an emergency stop by preventing what?
fact: ABS stands for anti-lock braking system.

text: What kind of car does Mr Bean drive?
fact: His is a citron-green 1977 Mini 1000 with a matt black bonnet.

text: Until 2007, which part of Australia had no speed limit on its open highways?
fact: A general 110 km/h limit came in that January, with higher limits on four highways.

text: Which German car maker has owned Rolls-Royce Motor Cars since 2003?
fact: Volkswagen outbid BMW in 1998 but came away with Bentley, not the Rolls-Royce name.

text: In 2008, which Indian company bought Jaguar and Land Rover from Ford?
fact: The sale was completed on 2 June 2008.

text: The name Subaru and the stars on its badge refer to what?
fact: Subaru is the cluster's Japanese name. The badge shows six stars.

text: What unusual type of engine powered the Mazda RX-7?
fact: The RX-7 was built from 1978 to 2002, over three generations.

text: Ford Australia designer Lew Bandt is credited with creating which kind of vehicle in 1934?
fact: A farmer's wife had asked for a car to go to church in and to carry pigs to market.

text: In Mad Max, Max's black Pursuit Special is a modified version of which Australian car?
fact: It began life as a white 1973 XB GT hardtop.

text: In The Fast and the Furious (2001), Dom's late father's muscle car is a 1970 what?
Top Gear drowned it, set it alight and blew up a tower block under it. Which ute still ran?
fact: The two episodes went to air in late 2003.

text: Which kind of engine ignites its fuel by compression alone, with no spark plugs?
fact: Squeezing the air in the cylinder makes it hot enough to light the fuel.

text: The Mercedes car brand was named after whom?
fact: Mercédès Jellinek's father Emil sold Daimler cars and raced them under her name.

text: Which Japanese car did Australia's Wheels magazine nickname "Godzilla" in 1989?
fact: The name was given to the R32 model in the magazine's July 1989 issue.

text: In 1964, Donald Campbell set a land speed record of 403 mph on which Australian salt lake?
fact: His car was the Bluebird-Proteus CN7, which drove all four wheels.

text: When an electric car slows by regenerative braking, what does its motor act as?
fact: The energy it recovers goes back into the battery.

text: The modern three-point seatbelt, designed by Nils Bohlin, first appeared in 1959 on which make?
fact: The company left the patent open so that every car maker could use the design.

text: Since 2007, the British MG badge has belonged to which Chinese car maker?
fact: Nanjing Automobile bought MG in 2005 and merged into SAIC two years later.

text: Holden's last Australian car factory was in which suburb?
fact: Ford's last car line was at Broadmeadows and Toyota's at Altona, both in Melbourne.

text: Which 1970s Australian car was known for a boot big enough to hold a 44-gallon drum?
fact: It was launched in 1973 and built at Zetland in Sydney.

text: In the mid-2000s, the Holden Monaro was sold in the United States as which car?
fact: It was sold there from 2004 to 2006. In Britain it was the Vauxhall Monaro.

text: Porsche first showed the 911 as the 901. Which car maker's objection forced the new name?
fact: It held the French rights to three-digit car names with a zero in the middle.

text: Where does the name of the Lamborghini Countach come from?
fact: Designer Marcello Gandini said a workman on the prototype used the word all the time.
wrong: A hot wind off the Sahara

text: Before it built cars, the Chinese company BYD began in 1995 making what?
fact: BYD is based in Shenzhen. It moved into cars in 2003 by buying a small state-owned car maker.

text: In 2009, which Pacific nation switched from driving on the right to driving on the left?
fact: The change came at 6 am on Monday 7 September, with a two-day holiday to keep traffic light.

text: The world's first parking meter was installed in 1935 in which American city?
fact: It went into service on 16 July 1935.

text: In 1888, who made the first long-distance trip in a petrol car, about 100 km across Germany?
fact: She drove from Mannheim to Pforzheim with her sons Richard and Eugen.

text: Where was the DeLorean DMC-12 sports car built?
fact: The factory was at Dunmurry, a few miles from the centre of Belfast.

text: In 2013, who bought the Lotus submarine car from The Spy Who Loved Me at a London auction?
fact: It had turned up in a Long Island storage unit that was sold unopened for about $100.

text: Honda's VTEC variable valve system first appeared in 1989 in which model?
fact: VTEC changes valve timing and lift at high revs. The Civic and CR-X got it five months later.

text: How many sides does an Australian stop sign have?
fact: Japan's stop sign is different: a red triangle pointing down.

text: In what year did Holden build its last car in Australia?
fact: The last Commodore came off the line on 20 October. Toyota had stopped 17 days earlier.

text: How many cylinders does the engine of the Bugatti Veyron have?
fact: They are laid out in a W and fed by four turbochargers.

text: What is the national speed limit for cars on a British motorway, in miles per hour?
fact: That is about 113 km/h.

text: On German autobahn stretches with no speed limit, what top speed is officially advised?
fact: It is the Richtgeschwindigkeit, a recommendation only: driving faster is not an offence.

text: In what year was the first Holden car launched?
fact: Prime Minister Ben Chifley was at the launch on 29 November.

text: In what year did Sweden switch from driving on the left to driving on the right?
fact: The change was made at 5 am on Sunday 3 September, known as Dagen H.

text: Japan's tiny kei cars may have an engine of up to how many cubic centimetres?
fact: The limit was raised from 550 cc in 1990.

text: How many laps of Mount Panorama make up the Bathurst 1000?
fact: One lap is about 6.2 km. The race has been run over 1000 km since 1973.

Which singer was born Stefani Germanotta?
fact: Her stage name comes from the Queen song Radio Ga Ga.

text: Rihanna launched which make-up brand, named for her surname, in 2017?
fact: She was born Robyn Rihanna Fenty. The range launched with 40 shades of foundation.

text: Which reality star co-founded the shapewear brand Skims?
fact: She founded it in 2019 with Jens Grede. Emma Grede was a founding partner.

text: Finneas O'Connell co-wrote and produced the hit albums of which pop star, his younger sister?
fact: The pair shared Oscars for the songs No Time to Die and What Was I Made For?

text: Which country music legend was Miley Cyrus's godmother?
fact: Parton also played Aunt Dolly in Miley's TV series Hannah Montana.

text: "Alright, alright, alright" is the catchphrase of which actor?
fact: He made the line up on the set of Dazed and Confused (1993).

text: Timothée Chalamet played which singer in the 2024 film A Complete Unknown?
fact: The film builds to the singer going electric at the 1965 Newport Folk Festival.

text: Which Friends star joined Instagram in October 2019 and gained a million followers in about five hours?
fact: Her first post was a photo with her Friends co-stars. Guinness timed it at 5 hours 16 minutes.

text: Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney (now Rob Mac) became co-owners of which Welsh football club in 2021?
fact: The takeover was agreed in November 2020 and completed the following February.

text: Who was Time magazine's Person of the Year for 2023?
fact: It was the year her Eras Tour began, in Glendale, Arizona.

text: Which actor co-founded Casamigos tequila, sold to Diageo in 2017 for up to US$1 billion?
fact: He started it with friends Rande Gerber and Mike Meldman. The name means "house of friends".

text: Which actor launched the UN's HeForShe campaign with a speech in New York in 2014?
fact: She spoke at UN Headquarters as a UN Women Goodwill Ambassador, a role she took up that year.

text: In 2018, who became the first Black man to win an Emmy, Grammy, Oscar and Tony, all in competition?
fact: He shared the win that sealed the set with Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice.

text: Stranger Things star Maya Hawke is the daughter of Ethan Hawke and which actor?
fact: Her parents met while making the 1997 film Gattaca.

text: Dannii Minogue was a judge on the UK version of which talent show from 2007 to 2010?
fact: Over the same years she was also a judge on Australia's Got Talent.

text: Harpo, the name of Oprah Winfrey's production company, is also her character's husband in which film?
fact: Harpo is also Oprah spelled backwards. She set the company up in 1986, the year after the film.

text: Keanu Reeves was born in which city?
fact: He was raised in Toronto and began acting on Canadian television.

text: Who became the first man to appear alone on the cover of American Vogue, on its December 2020 issue?
fact: He wore a blue Gucci dress for the cover photo.

text: Margot Robbie co-founded which production company, which made I, Tonya and Barbie?
fact: It was founded in 2014. Its other films include Promising Young Woman and Saltburn.

text: Chris Hemsworth married which Spanish actor in 2010?
fact: She played Elena Neves in the Fast & Furious films.

text: In the 2024 biopic Better Man, singer Robbie Williams is shown on screen as what?
fact: Williams has said he saw himself as a "performing monkey", which gave the film its idea.

text: Which Australian model was crowned Miss Universe in Quito, Ecuador, in 2004?
fact: She was Australia's second Miss Universe, after Kerry Anne Wells in 1972.

text: Which Australian played Elvis Presley in Sofia Coppola's 2023 film Priscilla?
fact: He was born in Brisbane and first found fame in Netflix's The Kissing Booth.

text: Which actor played "Uncle Sam" in Kendrick Lamar's 2025 Super Bowl half-time show?
fact: SZA and Serena Williams also made appearances.

text: Fans of which singer call themselves the Lambily?
fact: It blends "lamb", her pet name for fans, with "family".

text: Dakota Johnson's grandmother played the lead, Melanie Daniels, in which classic thriller?
fact: Her grandmother is Tippi Hedren. Dakota's parents are Melanie Griffith and Don Johnson.

text: In 2012 Stanley Tucci married the sister of which of his co-stars in The Devil Wears Prada?
fact: He married Felicity Blunt, a literary agent he had first met at the film's premiere.

text: Elton John completed an EGOT (Emmy, Grammy, Oscar, Tony) in 2024 by winning which award?
fact: It was for the concert special Elton John Live: Farewell from Dodger Stadium.

text: Whose Hollywood Walk of Fame star is mounted on a wall, not set in the pavement?
fact: He did not want the name he shares with the Prophet to be walked on.

text: Isla Fisher grew up in Perth, but in which country was she born?
fact: Her Scottish father was working in Muscat as a banker for the United Nations.

text: In 2024, who became the first Australian actor to receive the AFI Life Achievement Award?
fact: The tribute was set for June 2023 but a writers' strike pushed it back to April 2024.

text: Which Australian actor, who grew up in Geelong, was born Amanda Rogers?
fact: She took the name at 15, borrowing Portia from Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice.

text: As of the 2026 Oscars, who is the youngest man to have won Best Actor?
fact: He was 29 when he won for The Pianist in 2003. He won again in 2025 for The Brutalist.

text: Sarah Snook won a 2025 Tony for playing all 26 roles in a stage version of which novel?
fact: The show began at the Sydney Theatre Company. She also won an Olivier for it in London.

text: Before his pop career, Troye Sivan played the young version of which hero in a 2009 film?
fact: He played James Howlett, the boy who grows up to be Logan, in X-Men Origins: Wolverine.

text: Which singer walked the carpet at the 2019 Met Gala dressed as a lit-up chandelier?
fact: Later that night she changed into a hamburger costume.

text: As of the 2026 ceremony, how many Oscars has Leonardo DiCaprio won?
fact: He won Best Actor for The Revenant, on his fifth acting nomination.

text: Adele's first four albums are named for her age. What number is the title of the 2021 one?
fact: It followed 19, 21 and 25.

text: In what year did Billie Eilish, aged 20, become the youngest solo act to have headlined Glastonbury?
fact: She topped the Pyramid Stage bill on Friday 24 June. She had first played the festival in 2019.

text: In what year did Hugh Jackman host the Academy Awards?
fact: He had already hosted the Tony Awards three years running, from 2003 to 2005.

text: In what year did Oprah Winfrey give a new car to everyone in her studio audience?
fact: All 276 audience members got a Pontiac G6, to shouts of "You get a car!"

text: In what year did David and Victoria Beckham marry?
fact: The wedding was at Luttrellstown Castle in Ireland on 4 July.

text: In what year did Bindi Irwin win the American TV contest Dancing with the Stars?
fact: She was 17. Her brother Robert won the same show ten years later, in 2025.

text: In what year did People magazine name its first "Sexiest Man Alive"?
fact: Hugh Jackman (2008) and Chris Hemsworth (2014) later took the title.

text: In what year did Madame Tussauds open its wax museum at Sydney's Darling Harbour?
fact: It opened that April. Dannii Minogue's wax figure was unveiled ahead of the launch.

fact: It shares its name with Mokha, an old coffee-trading port in Yemen.

text: Order a "latte" in Italy and you are likely to be handed a glass of what?
fact: Latte is simply the Italian word for milk. The coffee is a caffè latte.
